lesson.title: Two Number Lines, One Address System: The Coordinate Plane
lesson.summary: The coordinate plane combines a horizontal and vertical number line into a two-dimensional grid divided into four quadrants.
lesson.body:
A single number line, the coordinate system you already know, can pin down the location of a point using only one number, because every position on that line is either to the left or right of zero by some distance. The coordinate plane extends that same idea into two dimensions by combining two number lines that cross at a right angle: a horizontal x-axis and a vertical y-axis, meeting at a shared zero point called the origin.

The two axes divide the coordinate plane into four regions called quadrants, numbered counterclockwise starting from the upper right. In Quadrant I, both coordinates are positive. In Quadrant II, the x-coordinate is negative and the y-coordinate is positive. In Quadrant III, both coordinates are negative. In Quadrant IV, the x-coordinate is positive and the y-coordinate is negative. Points that land exactly on the x-axis or y-axis are not considered part of any quadrant, since a quadrant requires both coordinates to be strictly positive or negative.

Consider four points: (3, -2), (-4, 5), (-1, -6), and (0, 3). The point (3, -2) has a positive x-coordinate and a negative y-coordinate, so it lies in Quadrant IV. The point (-4, 5) has a negative x-coordinate and a positive y-coordinate, so it lies in Quadrant II. The point (-1, -6) has both coordinates negative, so it lies in Quadrant III. The point (0, 3) has an x-coordinate of exactly 0, so it lies on the y-axis itself, not inside any quadrant at all.

The reason a single number line is not enough for most real situations is that many quantities need two independent pieces of information to describe a location, not just one. A city map needs both how far east or west and how far north or south a place is; a graph of a function needs both an input value and the output that goes with it. The x-axis and y-axis supply exactly those two independent measurements, one horizontal and one vertical, and because the axes are perpendicular, moving along one of them never changes your position along the other.

The origin itself, located at (0, 0), is the one point that belongs to both axes at once, and it serves as the starting reference for every measurement on the plane: distances and directions to any other point are always described relative to this single fixed spot. Grid lines are typically drawn at even, consistent intervals along both axes to make plotting and reading coordinates easier, and while the scale does not have to be the same on both axes, keeping it consistent avoids distorting the true shape of whatever is graphed on top of it.

Every location on the coordinate plane can be described precisely using two numbers, one for each axis, and the next chapter formalizes exactly how those two numbers are written and read together, as an ordered pair, which is the address system that the entire rest of this course relies on for plotting points, sketching functions, and reading graphs.
